passage:
So you asked what I'm like as a friend? Honestly, confusing. When Trisha's grandmother died last month, she told me at the bus stop and I just started crying. More than her, even. My throat closed up and I couldn't say one useful thing. I felt everything and did nothing.
Ved was there too. He was so calm. He said, 'You must be exhausted. Do you want us to walk you home?' Exactly the right thing. But later he admitted he didn't really feel much. He just worked out what she needed.
We talked about it afterwards, me and Ved. I'm trying to learn his part, the what-to-do part. He says he's trying to let himself feel mine.
Trisha told me later, 'Sahil, I was glad you both came.'

qa.q: Where did Trisha tell Sahil about her grandmother?
qa.a: At the bus stop.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling at the bus stop, and why couldn't Sahil help more?
qa.a: Sahil was overwhelmed by sadness, throat closing and crying, so there were no useful words left.

qa.q: What choice are Sahil and Ved making after talking it over?
qa.a: Sahil is trying to learn Ved's what-to-do part, and Ved is trying to let himself feel more, each practising the skill the other has.

qa.q: What might Trisha have needed from each friend?
qa.a: Trisha may have valued Sahil's shared tears and Ved's calm offer to walk her home, which is why she was glad both came.

grounding: Shows one teenager who feels a friend's pain deeply but is stuck, and another who understands clearly but stays detached, both working to grow.

passage:
I sit behind Samir in Class 10, so I saw most of it. When the football list went up, Deepak's name wasn't on it. He sat by the lockers, head down.
Samir walked over and said, very exactly, 'You're disappointed. Probably embarrassed too, since everyone saw the list.' Deepak nodded. Then Samir said, 'Anyway, want to see the new level I unlocked?' and turned his phone around.
Deepak's face shut like a door.
I don't know what Samir was thinking. Maybe he just didn't know what else to do. But the next morning I saw him sit down beside Deepak at the gate and say something quietly. They stayed there till the bell. Deepak even laughed once.

qa.q: Where did Deepak sit after the football list went up?
qa.a: By the lockers, head down.

qa.q: What does Deepak's face shutting like a door suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt brushed off and more hurt when Samir switched to the game right after naming his feelings.

qa.q: What choice did Samir make the next morning, and what changed?
qa.a: He sat beside Deepak at the gate and talked quietly till the bell, staying with the feeling this time, and Deepak even laughed.

qa.q: How might Deepak see Samir after the next morning?
qa.a: Deepak may see that Samir does care, even if it came out wrong at first, because he came back and stayed.

grounding: Shows, through a classmate's eyes, a teenager who reads feelings accurately but stays detached, and who begins to practise staying with someone who is hurt.

passage: When Raju's family lost their whole cotton crop to the hailstorm, the news went round the village school in Yavatmal by morning. Avni cried at the back of the class, and at lunch she couldn't eat; she kept saying, "Poor Raju, poor Raju," but when Raju walked past, she looked away, not knowing what to say. Vandana, her cousin, felt oddly calm. She understood exactly what the loss meant: fees, loans, his sister's wedding. She went straight up to Raju, asked what he needed, and wrote out the notes he'd miss while helping in the fields. Only later, walking home, did Vandana wonder why her chest felt so quiet, and Avni's so full.

qa.q: What destroyed Raju's family's crop?
qa.a: The hailstorm.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel on the walk home?
qa.a: She felt puzzled and a little uneasy, wondering why her chest felt so quiet while Avni's felt so full.

qa.q: How did Vandana's kind of empathy help Raju?
qa.a: Her clear understanding led her to ask what he needed and write out the notes he would miss.

qa.q: How might Raju feel when Avni looks away?
qa.a: Raju may feel alone or awkward, not knowing that Avni is actually deeply upset for him.

grounding: Illustrates a teen who understands a friend's loss clearly but feels detached, beside a cousin who feels deeply but freezes.

passage: When Mina's old dog Bruno died, Vera heard at the bus stop in Prague and burst into tears before Mina did. She hugged Mina so hard their glasses clashed, and cried the whole ride to school, until Mina ended up comforting her. At lunch their classmate Tomas, who usually seemed cool and far away, asked Mina calmly, "Do you want to talk about him or not talk about him?" Mina said, "Not talk." Tomas nodded and changed the subject to football, and Mina looked relieved. Vera watched, confused. She had felt everything and helped with nothing. Tomas had felt little, she guessed, and helped exactly. That evening Vera wrote in her notebook: "Next time, ask first."

qa.q: What was the dog's name?
qa.a: Bruno.

qa.q: How did Vera feel watching Tomas help Mina?
qa.a: Vera felt confused and a little ashamed, having felt everything but helped with nothing.

qa.q: What did Vera learn to try next time?
qa.a: To ask the person what they need first, the way Tomas did.

qa.q: How might Mina have felt when she ended up comforting Vera?
qa.a: Mina may have felt tired and a bit burdened, needing comfort herself.

grounding: Shows a teen who feels a friend's pain intensely but helps poorly, learning from a classmate who understands calmly.

passage:
At break in the school library, Neel told his classmates that his dog had died the night before.
Uday's eyes filled at once. His throat tightened so much he couldn't say a word, and he stared at the table, wishing he knew what to do.
Shankar nodded. "That's rough. Grief takes a while, right? Did you get to say bye?" Then he opened his chemistry book again.
Later, in the peer-support club, Ms Fernandes asked them both about it. "I felt it like it was my own dog," Uday said. "But I was useless."
"I knew what he was going through," Shankar admitted. "I just didn't feel much."
Ms Fernandes smiled. "Two halves of one skill. Uday, try saying one simple sentence. Shankar, try staying with him a minute longer." They agreed to practise at the next club meeting.

qa.q: What did Neel tell his classmates at break?
qa.a: He told them that his dog had died the night before.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when Neel shared the news?
qa.a: Uday felt Neel's pain deeply, with tears and a tight throat, but also felt helpless because he didn't know what to do.

qa.q: What small step did Ms Fernandes suggest to each of them?
qa.a: She asked Uday to try one simple sentence and Shankar to stay with Neel a minute longer, so each could build the half of empathy that was missing.

qa.q: How might Neel have seen Shankar going back to his chemistry book?
qa.a: Neel may have felt a little brushed off, even though Shankar's words showed real understanding.

grounding: Uday feels his classmate's pain but freezes while Shankar understands but stays detached, and a teacher shows both can practise their skills.
